title: The Plastic We Cannot See
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Global plastic production has grown rapidly since the 1950s, and a great deal of what is made is thrown away within a few years. Only a small proportion is recycled, so most ends up in landfill sites or in the environment. Plastic is durable, which is why it is so useful, and also why it is such a problem. Left in the environment, it does not rot; it breaks into smaller and smaller pieces. Those under five millimetres in length are known as microplastics, and they have now been found almost everywhere that scientists have looked, from the summit of high mountains to the deepest part of the ocean.

Microplastics fall into two groups. Primary microplastics are made small on purpose. They include the tiny beads once added to face scrubs and toothpaste, and the pellets, each about the size of a lentil, that factories melt to make plastic goods. Secondary microplastics are created when larger items, such as bottles, bags and fishing nets, are broken up by sunlight, waves and friction. Most of the microplastic in the sea is believed to be secondary.

Some of the largest sources are surprising. Clothes made from synthetic fabrics such as polyester shed tiny fibres every time they are washed, and a single load of washing may release hundreds of thousands of them. Car tyres are another important source, since the rubber contains plastic polymers and wears away a little on every journey. Together, these two sources are thought to account for a greater share of microplastic pollution than the beads in cosmetics ever did.

The route that fibres take is easy to follow. They leave the washing machine in the waste water and flow through the drains to a treatment plant. The plant removes the majority of them, which settle out as a thick substance called sludge. Unfortunately, the sludge is often spread on farmland as fertiliser, and rain can then wash the fibres into streams and rivers. From there they travel to the sea, where they are eaten by plankton, the tiny creatures at the base of the marine food chain.

Whether microplastics harm living things is still being studied. Dr Hannah Cole's team fed plankton with polystyrene beads and found that the animals ate less of their normal food and produced fewer eggs. Because small fish eat plankton, and larger animals eat the fish, plastic may be passed up the food chain in this way. Particles have also been detected in drinking water, in the air, and in samples of human blood. However, no study has yet shown that the particles inside our bodies cause disease, and scientists disagree about how worried we should be.

Professor Rafael Duarte believes that public alarm has run ahead of the evidence. Most laboratory experiments, he points out, expose animals to concentrations of plastic far higher than any found in nature, so their results may exaggerate the danger. He does not deny that plastic pollution is a problem, but he thinks that the attention given to microplastics distracts from larger plastic objects, which kill many more seabirds and turtles. Other scientists reply that waiting for certainty would be reckless, since the particles will remain in the environment for centuries.

Governments and industry have begun to act. Britain banned microbeads in rinse-off cosmetics in 2018, and France has passed a law requiring filters on new washing machines. Individuals can help by washing synthetic clothes less often, at lower temperatures and with a full load, all of which reduce the number of fibres released. Most researchers agree, however, that these measures only treat the symptoms, and that the real solution is to make and throw away less plastic in the first place.

items.q: Why are car tyres a source of microplastics?

They contain polymers and wear away as they are used.
They are broken up by sunlight.
They are washed into the drains.

items.q: What is Professor Duarte's main criticism of laboratory experiments?
o: They last for too short a time.
e: concentrations of plastic far higher than any found in nature

They deal with effects and not causes.
They are too expensive for governments.
They will not be adopted by industry.
